446.tx: We surveyed 521 UX practitioners about how they use AI at work and how it’s affecting them. The short answer: AI use is widespread and saves time, but practitioners are far from enthusiastic, and the benefits depend heavily on role, task, and workplace. TL;DR - Access was nearly universal (99%), but use of agentic AI ranged from 85% at startups to 36% at nonprofits. - Output quality (54%) and data privacy and security (50%) were the biggest barriers to AI adoption. 445.tx: People often use terms such as UX, UI, CX, and visual design interchangeably, even though they refer to different fields of practice. 1518.text: Your product is not the center of the universe October 19, 2026 • 4 min read Established products have a problem. They assume they’re the center of someone’s universe, and everything should feed through them. I’m going to call this a product-centric view. The product is at the center, everything else orbits it. I think this product-centric view has an expiry date. Once someone’s agent can work across all their tools, visiting each product one at a time starts to feel like friction. Coding and personal agents are bringing that date a lot closer. The products that thrive will take a different view. I’ll call this a person-centric view. It puts the person, along with their agent of choice, at the center. The agent pulls in the data, UI, and context from each product when it’s needed. Over time the agent builds up memory and preferences from across all of them, so the person never has to sta

The developers have a harder question: which parts of these screens actually exist? A concept image can communicate the feeling of a product while hiding the decisions that make it usable. That becomes dangerous when attractive visuals are mistaken for a working prototype. Generative tools such as Banana Pro AI can help teams explore visual directions through text-to-image creation and image-based variations, but they do not replace functional interface design. For founders, agencies, and software teams, the smarter approach is to label each kind of visual according to what it proves. A mood image proves that a direction is understandable. 925.tx: Studiogusto Unveils the Michelangelus Typeface The Michelangelus typeface decodes Michelangelo's handwriting into a humanist serif, commissioned by the Vatican and shipping with Microsoft 365. The family reads like the Renaissance itself, hand-inked and set down four centuries late. Lowercase letters keep the quill's logic: a wide-countered o that billows, an ink drop pooled in the bowl of the b, and every terminal ending in a gestural sweep instead of a hard stop. The capitals belong to another hand entirely, the chisel's. Studiogusto drew the uprights from Roman letterforms Michelangelo carved into stone, the sash of the PietÃ , the inscriptions of St. Peter's Basilica, the Sistine Chapel.

2585.text: We walk past myriad signs every day—building names, menus, logos, shop signs, symbols—without turning our heads or sparing them a second thought, but for Mumbai-based type designer and design educator Tanya George, noticing them is a 'default setting', as she tells STIR in a video conversation. A crooked letter, an unusual curve or a particularly pleasing arrangement of seemingly forgettable words can stop her in her tracks. Having worked in the field for over a decade—designing typefaces, logos, researching and writing about typography—George has built a practice around her fascination with noticing signs and lettering wherever she goes, and her instinct to see the world around her through the lens of type. 2757.text: Mistral and Nvidia are teaming up to speed up engineering simulations and industrial product design with AI. According to Mistral's announcement, the partners will combine the language model Mistral Large 4 and Mistral's physics AI with Nvidia's CUDA-X and Warp software libraries and Omniverse for 3D simulations. The goal is to link design, simulation, and AI training in one continuous workflow for industries like aerospace, automotive, and semiconductors. The companies also plan to release public benchmarks and open datasets for testing and comparing physics models and AI agents that work with engineering software. The two previously built Mistral NeMo together, and they're working on an open foundation model as part of the Nemotron Coalition. 2279.ogd: Microsoft introduces Reactor, a new C# framework that simplifies native Windows 11 app development without XAML.
2279.text: Microsoft is experimenting with Microsoft.UI.Reactor, a new C# framework that lets developers build native Windows 11 applications without writing XAML. The framework aims to simplify Windows app development, particularly for developers familiar with React, React Native, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose. Microsoft.UI.Reactor builds on top of WinUI and uses existing Windows interface controls rather than introducing a separate rendering engine. Traditional WinUI development requires developers to work with both XAML for interface design and C# for application logic. Reactor allows them to describe the entire interface directly in C#, reducing the need to manage multiple files and learn another language. 2440.text: Nigerian software engineer and technology entrepreneur Samuel Cousin has launched Naki UI, an open-source design system created for Jaspr, a web framework that allows developers to build websites using the Dart programming language. Released on pub.dev in September, Naki UI gives developers more than 75 reusable interface components and design utilities for creating modern web products. The project’s message — “Same familiar patterns. 1222.tx: Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy. Key findings - Anthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ six to one. - As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. 1219.title: Everyone is starting over
1219.rss_desc: The careers that thrive now are the ones willing to become someone new, over and over.
1219.ogt: Everyone is starting over — Gabriel Valdivia
1219.text: It’s a Tuesday afternoon on a Zoom call, and someone asks me a question that hangs in the air: “If you were to start over again today, what skills, tools, or frameworks would you focus on learning?” I glance out the window. It’s getting brisk. The sun feels brighter and sharper, the warmth that once felt like a bath now stings like a knife to my pupils. The green in the leaves is decaying into bright orange, a loud gasp before the fall. Inside the call, everyone waits for my answer. Outside, everything is becoming something else. I don’t hear that question as advice for some earlier version of me, stepping into the world after years of incubation in college. It’s the question rattling around in the head of every designer whose hair is now more gray than not. The careers that thrive now are the ones willing to become someone new, over and over. 2725.text: In a seismic shift for the global gaming industry, Electronic Arts (EA) has officially confirmed the shutdown of BioWare, the revered Canadian development studio responsible for some of the most influential role-playing games (RPGs) in history. The closure, announced on October 21, 2026, spells the end for a studio that shaped the narrative and character-driven gameplay for millions of fans worldwide, including a massive following in India. Alongside the studio's closure, EA has also made the decision to cease development on the next instalment of the Mass Effect franchise, a title that was in active development and widely anticipated by the gaming community. This move marks a profound and sudden end to an era for a studio celebrated for its rich storytelling and immersive universes. 1836.tx: We’ve built 10 different AI products at PostHog, including PostHog AI, our install Wizard, Replay Vision, Scouts, and more. They’re used by nearly 100,000 people every month. This is what we’ve learned. - AI can make your product worse. It can be slow and unreliable, or solve a problem nobody has (like chatting with your docs, any AI can do this). 1030.text: Redefine Properties’ Blue Route Mall in Tokai, Cape Town, has been awarded a Net Zero Level 2 certification by the Green Building Council South Africa (GBCSA), recognising the shopping centre’s progress in improving its waste management practices and reducing the amount of waste sent to landfill. A Net Zero Waste Level 2 certification focuses on the operational waste generated through the day-to-day use of a property. Under GBCSA’s current criteria, certification requires measured data showing that at least 90% of operational waste has been diverted from landfill over a 12-month period. 2011.text: Along India's coast, the boundary between land and sea is not always a line of concrete. In places, it is a forest of tangled roots, tidal channels, and sediment, a landscape that changes character with the water. Mangroves influence how water moves, how shorelines evolve, and how coastal communities experience flood risk. Their role in coastal protection depends on the width and condition of the forest, the movement of tides, and the accumulation of sediment. Seawalls and embankments are designed to resist water at a defined boundary. Mangroves work through a different set of processes. Their roots, trunks, and branches create resistance to moving water, while the forest interacts with sediment and tidal flows over time. When urban designers Nishita Parmar and Vedanti Agarwal studied the junction, they discovered something surprising. 189.title: National Urban Conclave 2026 inaugurated in Bhubaneswar, focuses on sustainable urban development - https://www.indiagazette.com/
189.rss_desc: National Urban Conclave 2026 inaugurated in Bhubaneswar, focuses on sustainable urban development https://www.indiagazette.com/
189.ogt: National Urban Conclave 2026 inaugurated in Bhubaneswar, focuses on sustainable urban development
189.ogd: The second edition of the National Urban Conclave 2026 was inaugurated in Bhubaneswar on Saturday, bringing together policymakers, urban development experts, industry representatives and other stakeholders to deliberate on India's urban transformation and sustainable city development. Organised by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs in collaboration with the Government of Odisha, the two-day conclave, being held on October 24 and 25, is themed "Urban Rising - Rethinking Urban Systems, Solutions and Delivery". According to the press release, Union Minister of State for Housing and Urban Affairs Tokhan Sahu inaugurated the event and emphasised the need to strengthen urban governance, improve infrastructure and ensure effective delivery of civic services. The conclave has brought together more than 1,200 participants to discuss key urban challenges, including affordable housing, sustainable mobility, water management, waste management and municipal governance. Addressing the gathering, Sahu highlighted India's growing urban population and the need for planned urbanisation to support the country's long-term development goals. India's urban population has increased from approximately 377 million in 2011 to around 500 million and is projected to reach 600 million by 2036, according to the PIB release. The conclave also highlighted the contribution of flagship government initiatives, including the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana, AMRUT, Swachh Bharat Mission, PM SVANidhi, DAY-NULM and the Smart Cities Mission, in strengthening urban infrastructure and improving citizens' quality of life, as per the information given by Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs. Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi highlighted the state's vision for planned urbanisation, modern infrastructure and sustainable mobility, aligned with the goals of Samruddha Odisha and Viksit Bharat 2047. He also outlined initiatives such as the expansion of Ama Bus services, the introduction of electric buses and the development of the Bhubaneswar-Cuttack-Puri-Paradip Economic Region to improve connectivity and promote regional economic growth. Odisha Chief Secretary Anu Garg stressed the importance of citizen-centric urban development, highlighting access to safe drinking water, efficient public transport, clean surroundings and accessible public spaces. The discussions on the first day covered seven thematic areas, including pedestrian safety, water and waste management, affordable housing, integrated urban infrastructure, urban service delivery, model building bye-laws and municipal law reforms. The sessions focused on improving pedestrian infrastructure, reducing water losses, promoting treated wastewater reuse, facilitating affordable housing and strengthening municipal finances and institutional capacity. Several initiatives and publications were also launched during the inaugural programme to support urban planning, capacity building, housing and municipal governance. These included the Urban Invest Window (UiWIN) Journal, the Samarthya Platform for the Central Public Health and Environmental Engineering Organisation (CPHEEO), and the ANKUR Handbook covering achievements for 2025-26 and reform priorities for 2026-27. The programme also featured the release of urban planning handbooks, housing-related resources and guidance on construction and demolition waste management. Officials highlighted the importance of financing and institutional reforms in meeting India's growing urban infrastructure requirements. Initiatives discussed included the Urban Challenge Fund, the Credit Repayment Guarantee Scheme and urban development-related reforms. NITI Aayog Chief Executive Officer Anurag Jain emphasised sustained coordination between the Centre and state governments to advance urban development, while underlining investment, institutional response and capacity building as key priorities. The conclave aims to provide a platform for exchanging ideas and identifying practical solutions to urban challenges as India moves towards its vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. The event will conclude on October 25. (ANI)

1189.tx: People in India have a complicated relationship with dirty walls. We often ignore potholes that last through several monsoons, unfinished buildings that stand for years, pavements that turn into parking spots, and tangled wires everywhere. But if a wall has torn posters, it quickly becomes a problem. Soon, someone shows up with a bucket of paint. The wall is made clean, primed, and given a new identity— it could be painted blue, green, or white. It might have a mural of a peacock, a banyan tree, a historical character, a dancing lady, or a kid tossing trash into a dustbin. 2675.ogd: Lion Green Road, a council-commissioned housing scheme in South London by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFFARCHITECTS, has won the 2026 RIBA Stirling Prize.
2675.text: Replacing a former car park, Lion Green Road transforms a challenging eight-metre change in ground level into an opportunity to rethink high-density housing. Delivering 157 homes across five residential blocks, the development creates a new connection between the busy Lion Green Road and the green parkland beyond. Rather than treating the site’s topography as a constraint, the scheme uses its changing levels and views to share a new residential environment. The five blocks are carefully positioned to work with the landscape, creating a shared setting for 635 residents that prioritises access to daylight, views and outdoor space. Although each block follows the same specification, subtle variations in height, orientation and position give the buildings distinct relationships with their surroundings. 1798.ogd: Engage with the 2027 Venice Biennale's call to Do Architecture, fostering a deeper connection between design and reality.
1798.text: "Architecture must return to its essence." With this statement, Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu establish the central premise of their curatorial vision for the 20th International Architecture Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, taking place from May 8 to November 21, 2027, across the Giardini, the Arsenale, and throughout Venice. Titled "Do Architecture – For the Possibility of Coexistence Facing a Real Reality", the exhibition calls for a return to the physical act of making architecture, at a time when, according to the curators, the discipline has become increasingly disconnected from lived reality through excessive abstraction, commercialization, and digitalization. 2022.tx: OMA dresses faceted French courthouse in coloured glass Dutch studio OMA has completed the Palais de Justice de Lille, a six-sided law court in northern France with a faceted facade lined with coloured glass. Located in Lille, the project was commissioned by the Ministry of Justice to host the city’s high and district courts. Palais de Justice de Lille occupies a verdant landscape adjacent to a star-shaped fortification, built in 1667 by the French military engineer Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban. 1825.tx: David Chipperfield Architects builds concrete gallery around singular artwork in Germany The Berlin office of David Chipperfield Architects has added a monolithic concrete gallery housing just one Anselm Kiefer painting to the grounds of the Carmen Würth Forum museum in Germany. Situated on a grassy mound in Künzelsau, the Anselm Kiefer Pavilion was built in the sculpture garden of the Carmen Würth Forum, an art museum and conference hall by David Chipperfield Architects that opened in 2020. The form of the gallery was determined by German painter Kiefer’s Schwarze Flocken, or Black Flakes, a large-scale artwork that had before been too large to exhibit in the museum. Rogério Renato Mateucci, 55, rector of Brazil’s Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, was killed when roofing material dislodged by strong winds struck him during a walking tour, according to Arizona’s Family. Scottsdale police are investigating the incident as a weather-related accident. The Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation has expressed condolences and confirmed the site's closure until further notice. 3004.text: The Minns Labor Government is moving ahead with plans to transform Bays West into Sydney’s newest waterfront suburb, bringing world-class design expertise together to help deliver thousands of new homes close to jobs, transport and the heart of the city. With twice as many young people leaving Sydney to find opportunities elsewhere, the Minns Labor Government is focused on delivering more homes in well-connected locations where people want to live, work and raise a family. Bays West is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to deliver up to 8,500 new homes, including at least 10 per cent affordable and essential worker housing, alongside parks, community facilities and beautiful new public spaces on Sydney Harbour. 618.tx: Concerns about the environmental impact of data centres have been popping across Canada almost as quickly as the data centres themselves. But what if there was a way to start lowering those emissions even before a facility is turned on? According to two cleantech advocates, greening the data centre boom starts with the buildings, and the huge amounts of concrete used to create them. 1467.text: The plant will make supersulfated cement, which has greater strength than other low-emission cement types and can cut CO₂ emissions by 93% compared to traditional cement. The plant was one of 77 projects in 27 countries chosen for funding out of 358 applications. The Innovation Fund is financed by revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System.

998.tx: ETH Zurich Department of Architecture researcher Karen Antorveza Paez has developed two digital manufacturing methods that use bacteria to bind sand into solid architectural elements. The research could offer an alternative approach to conventional cement-based construction, combining 3D printing and robotic fabrication. The project uses Sporosarcina pasteurii bacteria to produce calcium carbonate, or limestone, between grains of sand. The process, known as microbiologically induced calcite precipitation (MICP), creates mineral crystals that mechanically bind the grains together. The grounds undergo oil removal, drying and grinding before being blended and extruded into filament compatible with standard 3D printers, according to the team’s project presentation. 2850.ogd: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a $42.2 million small expenditure financing facility (SEFF) to develop the bamboo industry in India’s northeastern states, boosting agricultural productivity, strengthening rural livelihoods, and reducing dependence on imports.
2850.text: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a $42.2 million small expenditure financing facility (SEFF) to develop the bamboo industry in India’s northeastern states, boosting agricultural productivity, strengthening rural livelihoods, and reducing dependence on imports. The facility will support community-based projects that enhance the growth, usage, and management of bamboo resources across Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, and Tripura through multiple subloans financing a range of activities, including those ensuring the participation and employment of women across the value chain. It will also establish at least one women-led manufacturing facility in each state. “By harnessing the country’s abundant bamboo resources and building private sector-led industrial value chains, ADB’s financing will stimulate trade, investment, and infrastructure,” said ADB Country Director

2750.ogd: Rowland Keable, Director of Rammed Earth Consulting, makes the case for earth as an overlooked construction material, demonstrating how locally-sourced clay and soil can create durable, adaptable and genuinely circular buildings. Find out more by watching Rowland's talk here.
2750.text: Earth is one of the most abundant construction materials available, yet its potential is frequently overlooked in favour of timber, stone and manufactured alternatives. Drawing on more than three decades of experience in earth construction, Rowland Keable introduced the range of building techniques that make use of this resource, including rammed earth, compressed earth blocks, cob, light earth, clay mortars and plasters. Keable argued that earth’s greatest advantage lies in its circularity. Unlike cement-stabilised materials, unfired earth can be broken down, rehydrated and reused repeatedly without fundamentally changing its composition. He also highlighted the environmental benefits of using excavated material directly from construction sites, reducing waste and the need to import new products. 3025.text: Cleora, a 55-acre development in Salida, Colo., is expected to become one of the world’s largest planned 3D-printed residential communities that’s also its own metro district. Developed by Cleora with 3D-printing general contractor True North and technology provider RIC Robotics, the project will deliver single-family homes, duplexes, accessory dwelling units, and mixed-use spaces. Of the 106 homes planned, more than 65 will be constructed with RIC’s construction robotics and 3D-printing technology. Two autonomous RIC printing systems operate across the site. The project also includes a 3D-printed metro district, with infrastructure systems such as commercial, recreational, utilities, water treatment, and other essential services. 2228.tx: Bengaluru: Bengaluru may be enjoying cool weather now, but rising temperatures over the years have underlined the need to prepare for hotter temperatures. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has launched the Bengaluru Urban Heat Programme to protect pourakarmikas, ASHA workers, traffic police and other outdoor workers. Plans include cool roofs, shaded shelters and greener public spaces to offer relief when temperatures rise. Workers who clean streets, visit homes, manage busy junctions and staff dry waste collection centres spend hours in the sun. 539.ogd: Urban heat management requires integrated policies, ranging from housing planning, spatial planning, and health to disaster risk reduction.
539.text: JAKARTA - Urban heat requires more integrated handling, ranging from housing and spatial planning to health services and disaster policies. A number of initiatives to anticipate the impact of heat have been developed by local governments and various institutions. However, these efforts still face coordination, financing challenges, and have not integrated heat management within the framework of cross-sector policies. The findings of the Beyond Housing Types (BeHousing) research highlight three important foundations for building a city that is adaptive to heat, namely certainty of land rights, adaptive building design, and collaborative governance. All three need to be translated into concrete policies so that efforts to deal with the heat do not only depend on the ability of individuals and households, but are also supported by a protection system that reaches the most vulnerable people.

It has been nearly four years since 65 architects and design practices were handed a spot on London’s Architecture + Urbanism (A+U) framework. The conversation comes at a time when the boundaries between national and international education are becoming less distinct. For Indian schools, the question is increasingly not whether to choose a national or an international curriculum, but what kind of education will best prepare students for the opportunities ahead, both in India and globally. 2302.title: Beyond Grades: Clifton College’s Chris Stevens On Building Confident, Independent Learners - BW Education
2302.rss_desc: Beyond Grades: Clifton College’s Chris Stevens On Building Confident, Independent Learners BW Education
2302.ogt: Beyond Grades: Clifton College’s Chris Stevens On Building Confident, Independent Learners - BW Education
2302.ogd: Academic achievement remains an important measure of a student’s progress, but it does not capture everything that education is expected to deliver. Confidence, character, emotional well-being and the ability to think independently are equally important in preparing young people for life beyond school. For Dr Christopher Stevens, Executive Head of Clifton College and Clifton College Education Group, these elements must be part of the educational experience rather than treated as additions to academic learning.In an interaction with BW Education, Stevens discussed how schools can balance academic excellence with personal development, what Indian institutions can learn from British educational practices, and why teachers must continue to adapt as classrooms evolve. His perspective comes at a time when Indian schools are exploring new approaches to learning, including those encouraged by the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020.Clifton College’s partnership with Lighthouse Learning in India provides a context for this exchange, creating opportunities to share educational practices while recognising the distinct needs of Indian schools.Why Education Must Move Beyond Examination Results Stevens believes the purpose of education is best understood through the idea of an all-round learning experience. At Clifton College, he said, the objective is to provide an education that combines academic achievement with the development of character, and the skills students need to navigate their lives.“The key priorities for the group are in our charitable objects, and that's to provide an outstanding all-round education,” he said.This approach is particularly relevant in education systems where academic performance and competitive examinations have traditionally received considerable attention. While qualifications remain important, Stevens believes schools must also consider the conditions that enable students to learn effectively and develop confidence in their abilities.He places particular emphasis on students’ well-being and their sense of belonging within the school environment.“Well-being and the sense of belonging and the confidence that comes with that is actually the prerequisite for really effective learning,” he said.When students feel supported and confident, they are better placed to explore their interests, take on challenges, and develop the independence required for lifelong learning. For Stevens, this process extends beyond classroom lessons to include activities such as school plays, extracurricular pursuits, and other experiences that encourage students to work with others and apply what they have learnt.He argues that schools should not draw a rigid distinction between academic learning and activities outside the classroom. Both contribute to students’ development, even when the latter do not result in formal qualifications.The broader objective, therefore, is not simply to help students perform well in examinations, but to equip them with the skills and confidence to lead purposeful lives.What Indian Schools Can Learn From British Education Reflecting on his experience in India, Stevens noted that schools follow a range of educational approaches. Some place greater emphasis on traditional, knowledge-focused teaching, while others are adopting more experiential and progressive methods.He sees opportunities to build on this diversity, particularly as Indian schools work towards the learning approaches envisaged under NEP 2020.Drawing on his experience in the British independent-school system, Stevens highlighted classroom dialogue, Socratic questioning and the role of teachers as facilitators of learning. These methods encourage students to engage with ideas, ask questions, and develop their own understanding rather than rely exclusively on information delivered by the teacher.However, Stevens does not see international collaboration as a matter of simply transferring one country's educational model to another. He believes the exchange can help deepen practices that are already taking root in Indian schools.This distinction matters because educational approaches must respond to local circumstances, student needs, and institutional contexts. Rather than replacing existing practices, collaboration can help schools assess what works, identify areas for improvement, and adapt ideas to their own learning environments.Teachers Must Be Equipped To Understand How Students Learn Changes in classroom practices also place new expectations on teachers. As students encounter emerging technologies and bring different learning preferences to school, educators must be prepared to adapt their methods rather than rely solely on familiar teaching approaches.Stevens believes this requires professional development to be continuous. Teachers need subject knowledge, but they must also understand how to communicate that knowledge effectively and build relationships that support learning.“Teachers have to learn to master a particular field, but they need to be experts in pedagogy, experts in helping people learn,” he said.He emphasised that effective teaching involves understanding students’ motivations, building rapport with a class, and recognising that learners respond differently to teaching methods. This requires more than subject expertise alone. It calls for an understanding of student behaviour and the ability to respond to different learning needs.Stevens sees professional development as an ongoing cycle in which teachers continue to learn and refine their practices. Just as students need to become lifelong learners, educators must remain open to new ideas and approaches.International partnerships can support this process by enabling teachers to exchange experiences and learn from different educational settings. Such engagement can help educators reflect on their own practices and identify ways to make classroom learning more effective.AI Must Not Distract Schools From The Purpose Of Education Artificial intelligence is adding another layer of change to education, prompting schools to reconsider how students learn and how teachers deliver instruction. Stevens acknowledged the rapid pace of technological development and the need for educational institutions to remain forward-looking.At the same time, he believes schools must ensure that the adoption of new technologies does not overshadow the fundamental purpose of education.For Stevens, the goal is not merely to prepare students to acquire knowledge or secure qualifications, but to help them develop the confidence, judgement and capabilities needed to navigate an uncertain future.“The importance of education as something that purely delivers grades has got to shift to preparing people to have happy, purposeful and successful lives,” he said.This perspective places the emphasis on the individual behind academic results. Students must be prepared to participate in their communities, contribute to the organisations they join, and take responsibility as future leaders.Technology may change how knowledge is accessed and applied, but schools must continue to create opportunities for students to question, think independently and engage meaningfully with the world around them.Leadership Begins With A Willingness To Keep Learning Stevens’ emphasis on lifelong learning extends to educational leadership. He sees his role not simply as directing an institution, but as helping others become better leaders and creating the conditions in which effective learning can take place.This approach recognises that schools themselves must continue to learn. As educational expectations change, leaders need to remain open to new ideas, reflect on existing practices, and help teachers and students adapt.It also reinforces the value of dialogue between institutions and education systems. Partnerships can create opportunities to exchange perspectives, understand different approaches, and respond collectively to challenges that extend beyond national boundaries. These principles underpin the collaboration between Lighthouse Learning and Clifton in the recently launched PSG Clifton (a rebranding of the erstwhile Pathways School Gurgaon), where reciprocal benefit is anticipated for two highly successful schools. For Stevens, the future of education will depend on how effectively schools combine academic learning with the development of confident, independent, and adaptable individuals. New technologies and teaching methods will continue to shape classrooms, but their value will ultimately depend on whether they improve the learning experience.The central question for schools, therefore, is not simply how students perform academically, but whether the education they receive prepares them to think for themselves, respond to change, and lead fulfilling lives.

1285.text: In January 2020, the University of California's Standardized Testing Task Force finished an 18-month review of whether UC should keep requiring the SAT and ACT. Eighteen UC faculty from every campus spent a year working through UC's own admissions and academic-performance data. The findings surprised almost everyone. At UC, SAT scores were a better predictor of first-year college GPA than high school grades were. Test scores also predicted retention, four-year graduation, and cumulative UC GPA. Most counterintuitively, the report found that "test scores are better predictors of success for students who are Underrepresented Minority students (URMs), who are first-generation, or whose families are low-income." 874.text: A university admissions platform has emerged as a major source of frustration among the hundreds of thousands of students protesting across France in recent days. Placards calling for the abolishment of Parcoursup – sometimes in very strong language – have become a familiar sight on the streets. Students have accused the platform, which is similar to the UK’s Ucas system, of operating like a “black box” driven by “opaque” algorithms that reinforce social inequalities and leave young people in the dark about their future. In response to the protests, the French government has pledged to announce proposals to improve the system at the end of October. Parcoursup, which was introduced in 2018, is used by more than 900,000 students every year to apply for places at public universities, elite institutions such as grandes écoles, apprenticeships and other programmes. 1255.text: Sri Lanka clinched its first-ever Silver Medal at the 67th International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) in Shanghai, China. This historic milestone, marking 31 years of consistent participation, was led by Lasitha Jayasinghe of Royal International School, Kurunegala. Following the team’s return, Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya met the delegation at the Ministry of Education to celebrate their achievements and discuss their experiences on the world stage. Refusals of student visa applications averaged more than 2,500 a month in July, August and September, up from about 800 over the equivalent period last year. The increase coincided with reports of “increasingly sophisticated fraud” in student visa applications. Celia Coombes, visa director with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, said doctored bank statements and income tax returns were being used across “multiple” visa applications, sometimes in scams involving “hidden” agents. 1653.text: When AI can create polished products in seconds, we must redefine high achievement and reward students for genuine intellectual curiosity, not “automated perfection.” For generations, schools have rewarded the correct answer, the polished essay and other finished products of learning. Now that artificial intelligence (AI) can effortlessly write the papers and produce the results that used to come only from high achievers, what does “high achievement” mean? And which student behaviors should be rewarded? As someone who became a high achiever after years of low academic effort, my own school experiences remind me that it’s critical to consider how AI is affecting the full range of students in our classrooms — not only those who are struggling. 1654.text: With pandemic funding gone, districts are scrambling to maintain their “high-dosage” tutoring programs. Pandemic relief money paid for a big expansion of high-impact tutoring in schools. That money is gone, and districts now face a hard question: how to keep a tool proven to help students. Some districts have already cut back. Others have found ways to keep tutoring in place, but the school day is not getting any longer, and every change to a program has a cost. David Blazar, associate professor of education policy at the University of Maryland College of Education, studied tutoring programs in all 24 of Maryland's school districts. He tells Ira Apfel that the more likely outcome is not canceled tutoring but weakened tutoring, with bigger groups and fewer sessions that stop helping students as much. 1601.tx: A majority of Indian students believe artificial intelligence (AI) helps them complete tasks faster but are concerned that it perhaps prevent them from understanding and learning study material in depth, according to a survey by tech company HP. 1436.ogd: While women expressed an interest in starting businesses at nearly the same rate as men, the transition from aspiration to action remained uneven.
1436.tx: More than one in five Indian college students (22%) has already started a business, nearly matching the global average of 23%, according to the GUESSS India 2025 National Survey Report released by IIT Mandi in partnership with REVA University, Bengaluru. The survey, which covered 25,783 students from over 1,200 higher education institutions across 34 states and Union Territories, found that 43% of Indian students aspire to start a business, the same as the global average. Among students who have launched businesses, 35.5% reported generating regular sales, compared with 33% globally, indicating that a share of student ventures have moved beyond the idea stage to commercial activity. 1863.tx: Since OpenAI launched ChatGPT, the AI chatbot, in November 2022, employers across Asia have cut demand for workers in jobs more exposed to AI. The IMF’s October 2026 Regional Economic Outlook: Asia and Pacific offers some of the first empirical evidence of this shift, finding that employer demand in AI-exposed occupations fell by nearly 10% relative to less-exposed jobs. The International Monetary Fund’s report is based on 40 million online job postings from 19 low-income, emerging and advanced Asian economies. 2146.tx: For the longest time, aspiring engineers believed that if they could learn and master the art of coding, they would have multiple career opportunities. While this is largely true, the advent of AI has changed certain things. Syntax that once took an entire semester to master can now be generated in seconds by an AI model. What cannot be generated is judgment: the ability to decide what to build, why it matters, and how the pieces of a complex system fit together. This is the shift every Engineering student needs to internalise: Coding, as a standalone skill, is being commoditised. Architecting is becoming the premium. 2960.title: Green Field Factory, Bangladesh Wins RIBA Prize for Worker-Centered Design - Parametric Architecture
2960.tx: Most factories are designed around the efficient movement of materials and the supervision of labor. Green Field Factory in Rangpur, northern Bangladesh, was designed around a different priority: the daily experience of the people who work there. On 15 October 2026, the RIBA International Prize recognized that decision. Designed by Dhaka-based Nakshabid Architects for Karupannya Rangpur Limited, the seven-story textile facility employs approximately 5,000 people, the majority of whom are women. The jury, led by Bijoy Jain, called it a work of quiet humility and a redefinition of manufacturing architecture in South Asia and beyond.
